meta.review_cadence: Regulatory currency is a first-class property. Re-verify every regime object against primary sources at least quarterly; this landscape moves monthly (DORA/NIS2 amendments, UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill still in passage, EU AI Act reaching full application Aug 2026).
meta.purpose: Triage / applicability screening + high-level readiness scoring. NOT legal advice. Output determines which UK/EU digital-sovereignty regimes apply to a financial entity and roughly why, plus a maturity-stage readiness estimate. It qualifies a client into a deeper LTM advisory engagement (gap assessment + sovereignty roadmap).
meta.disclaimer: Indicative only. Applicability of law depends on specific facts and should be confirmed with qualified counsel. Grades of 'likely_confirm', 'partial', 'needs_legal_review' and 'advisory' explicitly signal where facilitated or legal validation is required.

delivery_tiers.tier_1_core: Self-serve web tool. Closed answer types only (single_select, multi_select, boolean, rating_1_5, range, with allow_not_applicable). Produces an INDICATIVE applicability + readiness result. This is the gated lead-gen path.
delivery_tiers.tier_2_extended: Consultant-led workshop. Adds richer types (drag_order, open_text) and deeper evidence probes. Produces a VALIDATED result that feeds the roadmap. Open text lives almost entirely here.

grades.applies: Trigger conditions clearly met. Regime is in scope.
grades.likely_confirm: Strong indication of scope; a fact needs confirmation (usually facilitated or legal).
grades.partial: Regime applies only in part — e.g. residual obligations after a lex-specialis carve-out.
grades.advisory: Not a hard applicability determination; a sovereignty risk/consideration to flag (e.g. residency != sovereignty).
grades.needs_legal_review: Fact pattern is ambiguous or high-stakes; refer to counsel before concluding.

rule_engine.note: Each regime carries an ordered array of applicability_rules. The engine evaluates every rule's 'when' condition tree against the collected facts; each satisfied rule yields its 'grade'. The regime's final grade = highest-precedence grade among satisfied rules. Every satisfied rule also contributes its 'rationale' to the explainability output (the 'why').
rule_engine.condition_tree: A condition is either a leaf {fact, op, value} or a group {all:[...]} / {any:[...]} / {not:{...}}. Trees nest arbitrarily.

maturity_spine.note: Readiness rolls up onto your five-stage sovereignty maturity model. Endpoints (Reactive -> Sovereign-by-Design) are fixed from your existing narrative; the three intermediate labels below are PROPOSED and must be reconciled against your Digital Sovereignty deck before this ships.

stages.label: Reactive
stages.descriptor: Compliance handled ad hoc and after the fact; sovereignty exposure largely unmapped.

stages.label: Aware (PROPOSED — confirm vs deck)
stages.descriptor: Obligations identified; controls patchy and undocumented.

stages.label: Structured (PROPOSED — confirm vs deck)
stages.descriptor: Defined controls and ownership; residency addressed but jurisdictional exposure not fully controlled.

stages.label: Managed (PROPOSED — confirm vs deck)
stages.descriptor: Controls tested and evidenced; third-party and concentration risk actively managed.

stages.label: Sovereign-by-Design
stages.descriptor: Sovereignty embedded in architecture and procurement; foreign-access risk provably mitigated, not just relocated.

scoring.readiness_question_normalisation: rating_1_5 -> ((value-1)/4)*100. single_select readiness options carry an explicit 'score' (0-100). range readiness questions map min..max linearly to 0..100.
scoring.regime_readiness: For each in-scope regime, weighted mean of its readiness_dimensions (each dimension = mean of its mapped questions * dimension weight), rounded to a 0-100 score, then mapped to a maturity stage via the bands above.
scoring.overall_sovereignty_readiness: Weighted mean of in-scope regime scores. Suggested regime weights favour the sharpest-teeth regimes for the vertical (see regime.weight). Only regimes graded applies/likely_confirm/partial contribute; advisory items surface as risk flags, not score inputs.

regimes.name: Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)
regimes.status_note: Applicable since 17 January 2025. 2026 is the first genuine supervisory enforcement cycle.

applicability_rules.rationale: Regulated financial entity operating in/into the EU falls within DORA's ~20 in-scope categories (Art. 2).

ICT providers to the financial sector can be designated Critical ICT Third-Party Providers (CTPPs) and placed under direct ESA Lead Overseer supervision. 19 CTPPs were designated as of Nov 2025 (incl. AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, IBM, Bloomberg).

obligations: ICT risk-management framework with board-level accountability.
ICT-incident classification and reporting — initial notification of a major incident within tight timelines (~4 hours after classification), tighter than NIS2.
Digital operational resilience testing, including threat-led penetration testing at least every 3 years for significant entities.
ICT third-party risk management: maintain a Register of Information of all ICT arrangements; assess and manage concentration risk; mandate contractual audit/access rights.
Documented exit strategies for critical ICT services.

regimes.name: NIS2 — residual obligations for financial entities
regimes.status_note: Enforceable since Oct 2024; first audits from June 2026. Jan 2026 Commission proposed targeted amendments. Transposition remains uneven across member states.

applicability_rules.rationale: DORA is lex specialis (DORA Art. 1(2) / NIS2 Art. 4): for financial entities DORA replaces NIS2's ICT risk-management and incident-reporting obligations. Residual NIS2 duties NOT covered by DORA (e.g. certain corporate-level cyber hygiene, cross-sector cooperation, and member-state registration such as Germany's registration requirement) may still apply. Exact residual scope varies by national transposition — confirm per member state.

obligations: Residual corporate-level cybersecurity obligations outside DORA's remit.
Member-state-specific registration/cooperation duties where applicable (varies by transposition).

readiness_dimensions.name: Corporate cyber hygiene beyond ICT-risk scope

regimes.name: UK Operational Resilience & Outsourcing (FCA/PRA)
regimes.legal_reference: FCA PS21/3 & PRA equivalent (operational resilience); PRA SS2/21 (outsourcing & third-party risk)

applicability_rules.rationale: FCA/PRA-regulated firms and FMIs must meet UK operational-resilience and outsourcing/third-party-risk rules. This responsibility is unchanged by the CTP regime — firms remain accountable for their own third-party arrangements.

obligations: Identify important business services and set impact tolerances.
Map and test the ability to remain within impact tolerances through severe-but-plausible scenarios.
Maintain a self-assessment document.
Manage outsourcing and third-party risk (due diligence, exit, contingency) per SS2/21.

regimes.name: UK Critical Third Parties (CTP) regime
regimes.legal_reference: FSMA 2000 (as amended by FSMA 2023); FCA PS24/16 / PRA PS16/24
regimes.status_note: Rules effective 1 Jan 2025; bind a provider only once HM Treasury designates it. First CTPs designated by HMT in July 2026. Treasury Committee recommended designating major AI/cloud providers by end 2026.

applicability_rules.rationale: ICT providers to the UK financial sector may be designated Critical Third Parties by HM Treasury, bringing them under joint FCA/PRA/Bank of England oversight (governance, supply-chain risk, cyber resilience, change and incident management, plus six Fundamental Rules). Obligations bind from the date of designation.

Reliance on a designated CTP is a material concentration/dependency consideration. The CTP rules bind the provider, not the firm — but the firm's own operational-resilience accountability is undiminished.

obligations: (If designated) Comply with CTP rules across governance, supply-chain risk, cyber resilience, change and incident management, and the six Fundamental Rules; provide assurance, testing and notifications to regulators.

sources.ref: Bank of England — regulators to begin overseeing CTPs
Morrison Foerster — UK CTP regime goes live

regimes.name: EU GDPR

applicability_rules.rationale: Processing personal data with an EU establishment, or targeting/monitoring individuals in the EU, engages GDPR (Art. 3). Includes Chapter V transfer restrictions and Art. 9 conditions for special-category data.

obligations: Lawful basis, transparency, data-subject rights, security of processing, records, DPO where applicable.
Chapter V restrictions on transfers of personal data outside the EEA.
Article 9 conditions where special-category data is processed.

regimes.name: UK GDPR / DPA 2018 / PECR (as amended by DUAA 2025)
regimes.legal_reference: UK GDPR; Data Protection Act 2018; PECR; Data (Use and Access) Act 2025
regimes.status_note: DUAA 2025 amendments are phasing in through 2026 (next commencement phase came into force 5 Feb 2026). EU->UK adequacy renewed to at least Dec 2031, so UK is not a 'third country' for EU personal data.

applicability_rules.rationale: Processing personal data with a UK establishment, or targeting/monitoring individuals in the UK, engages the UK GDPR / DPA 2018 (and PECR for electronic communications). Track DUAA 2025 changes as they commence.

obligations: UK GDPR / DPA 2018 core obligations (analogous to EU GDPR).
PECR obligations for electronic marketing/communications.
Monitor phased DUAA 2025 amendments.

sources.ref: Addleshaw Goddard — UK/EU data & cyber timeline

regimes.name: Cross-border transfer & jurisdictional-exposure (residency != sovereignty)
regimes.legal_reference: GDPR Chapter V (Schrems II, SCCs, TIAs); foreign-access statutes incl. US CLOUD Act; EU Data Act Art. on unlawful third-country access
regimes.status_note: This is the sovereignty crux, not a single statute. It probes exposure that persists even when residency requirements are met on paper.

applicability_rules.rationale: Residency is not sovereignty. A US-headquartered provider can be reachable under the US CLOUD Act regardless of where data physically sits (incl. EU/UK regions). Assess jurisdictional exposure and whether a genuine sovereign/EU-boundary control set is in place — not merely data location.

Personal data of EU subjects hosted outside the EEA in a non-adequate jurisdiction requires a valid Chapter V transfer mechanism (adequacy / SCCs + Transfer Impact Assessment). Note: hosting in the UK is covered by the EU->UK adequacy decision and is not, on its own, a transfer violation.

obligations: Valid transfer mechanism for personal data leaving the EEA/UK (adequacy, SCCs, BCRs).
Transfer Impact Assessments where required.
Demonstrable control against foreign-government access, not just data localisation.

sources.ref: GDPR Chapter V; US CLOUD Act (2018)

regimes.name: EU AI Act
regimes.status_note: Full application 2 August 2026; high-risk (Annex III) obligations apply from that point. GPAI obligations applied from Aug 2025.

applicability_rules.rationale: AI used for creditworthiness/credit scoring, or insurance risk assessment/pricing, is high-risk under Annex III — triggering risk management, data governance, transparency, human oversight and conformity obligations. Penalties reach up to 7% of global turnover.
Non-high-risk AI may still carry transparency and/or GPAI-related obligations depending on the system. Confirm classification.

obligations: (High-risk) Risk-management system, data & data-governance controls, technical documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight, accuracy/robustness, and conformity assessment.

regimes.name: EU Data Act
regimes.status_note: Applicable from 12 September 2025. Cloud switching/portability and safeguards against unlawful third-country access to non-personal data.

applicability_rules.rationale: Users and providers of cloud/data-processing services with an EU nexus fall within the Data Act's switching/portability duties and its prohibition on unlawful third-country access to non-personal/industrial data held in the EU. Confirm which obligations bind you as customer vs provider.

obligations: Cloud switching and portability facilitation (removal of switching charges phasing in).
Safeguards against unlawful third-country governmental access to non-personal data held in the EU.
Contractual fairness for data access/sharing.
